title: The Negus weeps
hook: Ja'far recites Surah Maryam, and the Christian king weeps and refuses to hand them over (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ja'far's speech before the king. Your line was: truth, kinship, mercy. Did you find your three sentences, and did anyone hear them? Day seven hundred forty-four.

Ja'far has finished. The court is quiet. The envoys from Mecca are waiting for the king to send the runaways home. His bishops have their books open around him. And the Negus asks one question. Not about politics, not about the gifts. He asks: do you have with you anything of what your prophet brought from God? Ja'far says yes. Read it to me, says the king. Ja'far has to choose, on the spot, which words to read to a Christian king in a Christian court. Today: al-Najashi.
screen: `THE COURT IS QUIET.` → `DO YOU HAVE ANY OF IT WITH YOU?` → `READ IT TO ME.`

segments.voice: Umm Salamah says Ja'far recited the opening of surah Maryam, the surah named for Mary. It tells of Zachariah praying in secret for a child in his old age, of John, and then of Mary herself. In Pickthall's words, a verse of it begins: "And make mention of Mary in the Scripture." It goes on to the angel who comes to her, and the birth of her son, Jesus. Look at the choice. Ja'far didn't read the passages a king might find hardest. He read the ones about the figures this court's own faith honored, as the Qur'an tells them. And Umm Salamah says the Negus wept until his beard was wet, and his bishops wept until the pages in front of them were wet. Then the king spoke. In her telling, he said that this and what Moses brought came from the same lamp; in Ibn Ishaq's version of the scene, it is what Jesus brought. And he turned to the envoys: go. I will not hand them over to you. Later he gave back the gifts Quraysh had sent. Umm Salamah has him say that he would not take a mountain of gold to harm a single one of them. Notice who the hero of this chapter is. Not a companion. A Christian king, who listened, was moved, and protected strangers who had nothing to give him. Muslims tell his story with honor. The tears came first. The protection followed.
screen: `HE READ THE SURAH OF MARY.` · `THE KING WEPT, AND THE BISHOPS.` · `I WILL NOT HAND THEM OVER.` · `NOT FOR A MOUNTAIN OF GOLD.`

segments.voice: The practice: protect a guest. Settle into your breath. Then think about who is a guest in your life right now: someone new at work, a family that just moved onto your street, a friend of a friend at the table, a relative staying with you. Who might they need protecting from? Loneliness, a joke at their expense, a rule they don't know yet. Picture one of them. Find one way, this week, that you'll stand between them and whatever makes them feel unwelcome. Hold that picture while you sit. The bell holds the time.
Al-Najashi. The Christian king of Abyssinia who hears surah Maryam, weeps, and refuses to hand the Muslims over, not for a mountain of gold. Today's word.
Your line: the king wept. Today, when someone new is in a room with you, be the one who makes sure they're not left alone in it. Day seven hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims honor the Negus, al-Najashi, in sirah lessons as the Christian king who sheltered the emigrants, and Ja'far's recitation of surah Maryam before him is retold as a story of shared reverence for Mary and Jesus.

original.note: Arabic: al-Najashi, the title the sources use for the king of Abyssinia, the Negus.

trapdoor: what you thought: a foreign king made a political decision.
what it means: a Christian king listened to the story of Mary, wept, and protected strangers at a cost.
what a scholar hears: Umm Salamah's report in Musnad Ahmad: surah Maryam, 'the same lamp', the gifts returned, the mountain of gold.

sources.ref: Musnad Ahmad 1740 (Umm Salamah: Ja'far recites surah Maryam; the Negus and his bishops weep; he refuses to hand them over and returns the gifts)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Negus: this and what Jesus brought come from the same niche)

notes: Pickthall 19:16 ('And make mention of Mary in the Scripture,') quoted from memory; confirm wording.
The report says Ja'far recited the beginning of Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad; the script says 'the opening' and lists what the surah tells without claiming exactly how far he read. Confirm.
The Negus's 'same lamp' (mishkat) remark is given as Umm Salamah's telling, in paraphrase. It is said by a character in a Muslim source; confirm the framing is fair to Christian listeners.
The second hearing (Amr's charge about Jesus, Ja'far's answer, the Negus and the stick) is deliberately left out to avoid a doctrinal comparison; a Keeper may want it on another day.
'Muslims have told his story with honor ever since' is a general claim; soften if needed.
Musnad Ahmad 1740 number cited from memory; confirm.

Editor: corrected the 'same lamp' attribution. Umm Salamah's report in Musnad Ahmad has the Negus compare it with what Moses brought; Ibn Ishaq's version has Jesus. The teach now gives both and Ibn Ishaq is added to sources. Also changed 'Think about the choice' to 'Look at the choice'. Confirm both wordings against the texts.

Auditor: hook now says the bishops have their books open (the report has the Negus summon his bishops, who spread their scrolls around him) instead of 'churchmen', to keep them distinct from the patricians of day 743.
